blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Analyse the consequences of protection for the home country and its trading partners, and judge when protection works.

blocks.heading: Inside the home country
blocks.text: With the blanket tariff in place for a year, the consequences at home divide by who is asked. Consumers: an imported blanket costs N$250 against N$200 before, and home blankets rise from N$210 to N$230 as import competition eases, so buyers pay more and choose from fewer brands. Home producers: output rises from 3 000 towards 3 800 blankets, and the jobs and income behind them stay. The government: 6 000 x N$50 = N$300 000 of revenue in the year. The wider cost: home firms facing less import pressure may put off cutting their own costs, and the economy keeps resources in an industry that buyers were moving away from.

blocks.heading: Across the border
blocks.text: The exporting country's blanket makers sell 2 000 fewer blankets a year, since 8 000 - 6 000 = 2 000, and the jobs behind those sales tend to go. Their government may answer with barriers of its own on Namibian exports - fish, beef, minerals - and each answer shrinks trade on both sides. Protection is rarely a home-only policy: its costs travel, and so does the retaliation it invites.

blocks.heading: Does protection work?
blocks.text: Judged as a whole, protection tends to help the sheltered industry in the short run while spreading its cost across the economy's consumers. It is likely to justify itself where the infant industry genuinely matures and the shelter is withdrawn on time, or where the dumping is real and temporary. It is likely to fail where the shelter removes the pressure to improve, where the protected industry never reaches scale, or where partners retaliate and both countries end up trading less. The condition that decides it: what the shelter buys, and whether it is taken away once it has bought it.
